title: The Economics of Credence Goods: An Experiment on the Role of Liability, Verifiability, Reputation, and Competition
pub: American Economic Review, vol. 101, no. 2, pp. 526-555
author: Uwe Dulleck · Rudolf Kerschbamer · Matthias Sutter

dup.label: economics credence goods an experiment on role liability verifiability reputation competition

sib.t: Verifiability, not difficulty, sets the order of automation

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source examines institutional safeguards and seller behaviour in experimental credence-goods markets, not legal AI capabilities, human verification, or workflow redesign. Its findings therefore do not provide enough direct evidence to determine a position on the cluster’s proposition.

st.t: Credence incentives: More information may not improve service
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s incentive-and-accountability framing and materially strengthens it with controlled experimental evidence: liability improves efficiency far more than verifiability, while competition increases trade and lowers prices without improving efficiency when liability is absent. This directly supports the claim that added information or market choice alone may not improve expert-service quality.
qs: While theory predicts that either liability or verifiability yields efficiency, we find that liability has a crucial, but verifiability only a minor effect.
Seller competition drives down prices and yields maximal trade, but does not lead to higher efficiency as long as liability is violated.

st.t: Credence exchange: Rules constrain but preserve discretion
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s procedural account: providers have transaction-specific information, buyers do not, and the action rules impose a mandatory choice for type 2 while preserving provider discretion for type 1. It also reports only the experimental design and incentives, not evidence that safeguards are effective.
qs: There are two possibilities a player A can have during choosing his action:     a) In case player B is a type 1 player, player A can chose either action 1 or action 2.
b) In case player B is a type 2 player, player A has to choose action 2.

st.t: Credence markets: Liability and verifiability remain hypotheses
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s cautious framing. Its figure fragments distinguish liability and verifiability conditions, separate treatment and charging outcomes from accepted prices, and label period-16 values as predictions. Because the supplied fragments preserve no readable comparative results, they support the analytical distinctions but not any claim that liability or verifiability is an established remedy.

st.t: Expert matching: Observable work may remain unsuitable
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition with experimental evidence: requiring sufficient treatment markedly improves trade and efficiency, whereas verifiability has almost no effect because observing delivered work does not establish whether it met the customer’s need. It also supports the conclusion that lower prices, greater trade and reputation are unreliable indicators of appropriate treatment.
qs: Liability to provide a sufficient treatment has been found to have a very strong effect not only on the likelihood of trade on our experimental credence goods markets, but also on its efficiency.
Contrary to our predictions, verifiability has been found to have almost no effect (compared to a situation where only moral norms may apply).

st.t: Service necessity: Verifiability cannot ensure proper treatment
st.an: The source directly supports the proposition by distinguishing observable service delivery from whether the service was appropriate, and by experimentally finding that verifiability had only a minor effect while liability more reliably improved trade and efficiency.
qs: credence goods have the characteristic that though consumers can observe the utility they derive from the good ex post, they cannot judge whether the type or quality of the good they have received is the ex ante needed one.
Verifiability of a seller’s actions, although theoretically as powerful as liability, has only a minor impact.

kp.k: Information asymmetry creates distinct forms of expert misconduct
kp.d: The authors examine credence goods such as medical treatment, repairs, software and taxi rides, rather than AI or legal services directly. Consumers may observe whether a service solves their problem without knowing whether the treatment supplied was necessary or even what was supplied. The framework distinguishes unnecessary costly treatment, insufficient treatment and charging for work not performed; fear of overcharging can also discourage subsequent trade.
qs: Moreover, consumers may even ex post be unable to observe which type or quality they actually received.
An expert seller, however, is able to identify the type or quality that fits a consumer’s needs by performing a diagnosis.
This case is referred to as overtreatment because the additional benefits to the consumer are smaller than the additional costs.

kp.k: Factorial experiment separates four institutional and market mechanisms
kp.d: The 2009 working paper reports a computerized experiment with 936 undergraduate students across 16 conditions, independently varying liability, verifiability, reputation and competition. Groups contained four sellers and four consumers, with fixed roles over 16 periods. Major treatment was needed with probability 0.5; sufficient treatment yielded 10 points, minor and major treatments cost 2 and 6 points, and the outside option was 1.6 points per participant. These are controlled laboratory findings, not observations of professional practitioners.
qs: A total of 936 undergraduate students participated in the experiment.
There are 16 periods of interaction between sellers and consumers in all conditions.
Four subjects in each matching group are in the role of consumers, and four in the role of sellers.

kp.k: Liability and verifiability constrain different dimensions of conduct
kp.d: Liability is implemented as a requirement to provide sufficient treatment, directly precluding undertreatment but allowing overtreatment and overcharging. Verifiability requires sellers to charge for the treatment actually provided, eliminating overcharging without ensuring appropriate treatment. This source's verifiability concerns observable service provision and billing, not human checking of AI output.
qs: Thus, liability prevents undertreatment, but it does not preclude overtreatment and/or overcharging.
As a consequence, verifiability prevents overcharging, but it does not preclude under- and/or overtreatment.

kp.k: Standard theory predicts either safeguard should ensure efficiency
kp.d: Under rational, own-money-maximizing preferences, the model predicts market breakdown in anonymous bilateral trade without either safeguard, but full trade and appropriate treatment when liability or verifiability applies. With verifiability alone, equal mark-ups should remove incentives to choose treatment according to profitability rather than need. In the baseline condition, the predicted price vector is {6, 10}, matching the treatment-cost difference of 4.
qs: Interaction always takes place if either L or V (or both) holds; otherwise the market breaks down.
In B/V sellers post the equal mark-up vector {6, 10}.
With interaction, prices are such that sellers are induced to provide the appropriate treatment and that the gains from trade accrue to the sellers.

kp.k: Liability substantially increases observed trade and efficiency
kp.d: Table 3 reports baseline consumer interaction of 45% without either safeguard, 50% with verifiability alone, and 82% in both liability conditions. Efficiency is respectively 18%, 16%, 84% with liability alone and 81% with both safeguards. Liability's effects on interaction and efficiency are statistically significant. The table defines efficiency relative to maximum possible average profit after subtracting the outside option, rather than simply as the share receiving appropriate treatment.
qs: Liability has a highly significantly positive impact on the frequency of interaction and on the degree of efficiency, as standard theory predicts.
Efficiency is below 20% without liability, but above 80% with liability.

kp.k: Verifiability alone fails to produce predicted efficient incentives
kp.d: Baseline verifiability produces no significant improvement in interaction or efficiency. Undertreatment is 60% with verifiability alone versus 53% without either safeguard. Sellers post equal mark-up vectors in only 4% of B/V cases, while 94% are undertreatment-incentivizing vectors. Neither the standard nor the non-standard preference model explains this poor aggregate performance.
qs: However, verifiability has no significant impact on those variables, contrary to the standard prediction.
In B/V we observe equal mark-up vectors in only 4% of cases (29 out of 704), while in 94% of cases sellers post an undertreatment price-vector.
Our model with non-standard preferences explains only the ‘better’ part of the latter result, but fails to account for the ‘worse’ part.

kp.k: Honesty partly sustains trade without institutional safeguards
kp.d: The non-standard model assumes heterogeneous aversion to undertreatment, overtreatment and overcharging. Supporting observations include 13 of 48 baseline sellers always providing appropriate treatment without either safeguard, and twelve of 48 always charging for actual treatment under liability despite opportunities to charge more. These patterns contradict universal opportunism, although they do not establish moral preferences as the sole explanation or resolve every model discrepancy.
qs: In fact, 13 out of 48 sellers always provide the appropriate treatment across all 16 periods.
In fact, twelve out of 48 sellers always charge for the actually provided treatment even when ph > pl.
Our simple model with non-standard preferences has been found to explain the behavior in credence goods markets in most cases better than a model with standard preferences.

kp.k: Consumers accept prices reflecting overly optimistic expectations
kp.d: Without safeguards, consumers accept average posted prices of 7.28 for major and 4.67 for minor treatment, despite the standard model's much lower acceptance threshold. Their average profit is only 1.00, below the 1.6 outside option; Table 3 reports 1.06 with verifiability alone, also below the outside option. The authors interpret acceptance as compatible with expectations of non-standard seller preferences, but find those expectations too optimistic on average.
qs: In B/N consumers accept price-vectors with average prices ph = 7.28 and pl = 4.67.
The average profits of consumers are only 1.00, however, which is less than their outside option and shows that consumers’ expectations are too optimistic, on average.
Rather, the low price lures consumers into the market.

kp.k: Reputation can increase trust without improving consumer returns
kp.d: Reputation is implemented through persistent seller identities and consumers' own transaction histories, not public reviews or complete market histories. Without competition or safeguards, it increases interaction from 45% to 63% and reduces overcharging from 86% to 53%, but does not significantly reduce undertreatment or improve consumer profits. Seller profits rise significantly. When liability or verifiability already applies, reputation generally has little aggregate effect.
qs: Table 4 shows a significant increase in the frequency of interaction in R/N, compared to B/N.
Likewise, overcharging decreases.

In sum, adding an opportunity for reputation building has only important effects when there are no institutional safeguards against sellers’ misbehavior (in R/N), but reputation benefits the sellers only.

kp.k: Competition lowers prices but does not reliably improve treatment
kp.d: Competition lets consumers choose among four sellers without search costs or seller capacity constraints. Accepted prices fall by about two experimental units, and trade increases across institutional conditions. Without either safeguard, interaction rises from 45% to 73%, while efficiency changes from 18% to 13% without a significant improvement. Undertreatment rises from 53% to 73%, but that difference is not statistically significant. Contrary to the abstract's broad wording, the detailed results report significant efficiency improvements from competition when verifiability alone applies: 16% in B/V versus 34% in C/V.
qs: Prices pl and ph are on average about 2 units lower with seller-competition than without
The impact of competition on efficiency is ambiguous, however.

In particular, efficiency is not increased by introducing C when liability and verifiability are both violated, but the impact is positive in all other cases although the effect is only significant in V.

kp.k: Competition redistributes surplus and concentrates customer demand
kp.d: With liability alone, Table 4 shows average seller profits falling from 3.44 to 1.23 and consumer profits rising from 2.12 to 4.56 when competition is introduced. More consumer participation can coexist with fewer sellers securing any customers: active sellers serve multiple consumers, leaving others without trade. Consequently, the negative competition coefficient in the seller-side interaction regression is not evidence that competition reduces total consumer participation.
qs: The gains from trade shift (almost completely) from sellers to consumers when shifting from a condition without seller-competition to one where sellers compete.

Competition has a significant negative main effect on the probability of a particular seller having an interaction, since it leads to a concentration of several consumers visiting the same seller, leaving more sellers without any consumer.

kp.k: Combining reputation and competition fails predicted quality improvements
kp.d: The standard model permits additional equilibria without safeguards in which reputation and competition support appropriate treatment during the first nine periods. Experimentally, adding reputation to competition increases interaction from 73% to 85% but does not significantly improve efficiency or substantively change prices and undertreatment. The authors therefore find no evidence for that particular reputation-supported equilibrium.
qs: We do not find evidence for this type of equilibrium, though, since adding reputation-building keeps both the undertreatment rate and the posted, respectively accepted, prices basically at the same levels as in C/N.
When liability or verifiability (or both) applies, adding an opportunity for reputation building to competition does not change any of the important variables substantially.

kp.k: Price differences shape treatment and billing misconduct
kp.d: The regressions and descriptive results support continuous responses to financial incentives, rather than the standard model's abrupt switches. Under verifiability, increasing the major-minus-minor price difference reduces undertreatment but increases overtreatment. Where overcharging is possible, it also becomes more likely as that difference grows. These findings support important components of the non-standard preference model, while showing that reducing one type of misconduct can strengthen incentives for another.
qs: This implies that the likelihood of undertreatment is decreasing in the price difference ph – pl, as expected from the non-standard predictions BNS1, RNS1, and CNS1.
The likelihood of overcharging decreases with the low price pl and increases with the high price ph, as implied by the non-standard predictions.

kp.k: Undetected misconduct weakens reputation relative to experience goods
kp.d: The authors compare their findings with Huck, Lünser and Tyran's experience-goods experiments, which reported stronger reputation effects. They propose that imperfect detection of cheating explains the difference: in their credence-goods setting, sufficient treatment need not reveal whether misconduct occurred. This is offered as a possible mechanism, not a separately identified causal finding.
qs: One possible explanation is that cheating is always detected in the set-up of Huck et al. (2007) – which makes a good reputation all the more valuable – whereas in our design cheating may remain undetected.
The latter possibility weakens the importance, and ultimately the effects, of reputation.

kp.k: Authors recommend sufficient-treatment liability over billing transparency
kp.d: The authors infer that liability clauses are the most suitable remedy among the mechanisms studied and argue that requiring evidence of work performed does not address the underlying treatment problem. They acknowledge that liability does not eliminate overtreatment or overcharging. This is a policy interpretation of an experiment in which sufficient treatment is compulsory, not a test of real-world litigation, enforcement costs or any legal-AI regulatory regime.
qs: Hence, our results suggest that legal liability clauses are most suitable to cure many of the inefficiencies associated with the provision of credence goods.
However, liability does not solve the problems of overtreatment (which may also create inefficiencies) or overcharging (which is another form of cheating on the consumer).

kp.k: Unexplained behavior motivates richer models of professional conduct
kp.d: The working paper identifies frequent overtreatment under equal mark-up vectors and the popularity of the {6, 8} price vector as unresolved findings. The authors suggest relative payoff concerns, reciprocity and guilt aversion as possible extensions. These remain proposed explanations and future research directions rather than experimentally established mechanisms.
qs: One natural extension would therefore be to include relative payoff concerns of agents in our model.
Another extension would be to consider concerns for reciprocity in sequential and repeated interactions

Though all of these extensions promise to increase our knowledge of which conditions lead to more efficient trade on credence goods markets, they are beyond the scope of this paper and are left for future research.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Dulleck, Kerschbamer and Sutter make claims about credence-goods markets, not AI or legal services: liability strongly improves trade and efficiency, verifiability alone has little effect, and competition increases trade primarily through lower prices.
pts.d: In the supplied working-paper version, the authors distinguish theoretical predictions from experimental findings. Standard theory predicts full efficiency with either liability or verifiability, but the experiment finds strong effects principally for liability. Reputation generally has limited effects; without either institutional safeguard, it increases trade and reduces overcharging but does not significantly improve efficiency. Competition lowers prices and shifts gains toward consumers, without reliably reducing mistreatment. Although the abstract states broadly that competition does not improve efficiency without liability, the detailed results identify an exception when verifiability alone applies. The authors also find that some sellers provide appropriate treatment despite incentives to cheat, and argue that a model incorporating moral or social preferences explains much, but not all, observed behavior better than a purely monetary model. These are cross-domain findings; the source does not claim that AI changes these relationships.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The primary evidence is a controlled, incentivized laboratory experiment with 936 undergraduate participants across 16 conditions, compared against formal equilibrium predictions.
pts.d: The experiment independently varies liability, verifiability, reputation and competition in a 2×2×2×2 design. Groups contain four sellers and four consumers interacting for 16 periods. In the baseline, trade frequencies are 45% without either safeguard, 50% with verifiability alone, and 82% in each liability condition. Corresponding normalized efficiency measures are 18%, 16%, 84% and 81%. Without liability, baseline undertreatment rates are 53% and 60%. With neither safeguard, competition raises consumer trade from 45% to 73%, while measured efficiency changes from 18% to 13%, not a significant improvement. With verifiability alone, competition raises trade from 50% to 88% and efficiency from 16% to 34%, a significant improvement. The authors use matching-group-level Mann–Whitney tests and random-effects probit regressions. Earlier studies of health care and repairs supply contextual evidence, not direct tests of AI or legal markets.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern a finite 16-period experimental market; the theoretical predictions depend on specified information, incentives and institutional constraints, not a calendar forecast.
pts.d: The supplied main text is the 2009 working-paper version, accompanied by the published article’s official supplementary material. Liability is implemented by preventing insufficient treatment, rather than by modeling litigation, damages or imperfect enforcement. Verifiability forces charges to match the treatment supplied, without revealing whether that treatment was needed; it is not human verification of AI output. Reputation consists of identifiable sellers and consumers’ own past experiences, not public reviews. Competition permits costless price comparison among four sellers with no capacity constraints. Standard predictions assume rational, own-money-maximizing participants and a commonly known end date; the official supplement additionally states risk neutrality. Alternative predictions allow heterogeneous moral preferences and particular consumer beliefs. Some reputation-and-competition equilibria predict appropriate treatment in early periods, but the experiment does not find evidence of the specified equilibrium. The authors’ recommendation for legal liability clauses is an extrapolation from this design, not a measured effect of an actual legal regime.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected parties are expert sellers and consumers of credence goods, exemplified by medical care, repairs, software and taxi rides in unfamiliar cities.
pts.d: Consumers cannot reliably determine the treatment they need or whether the supplied treatment was necessary, creating opportunities for under- and overtreatment and overcharging. Liability assures sufficient treatment and encourages participation, but does not eliminate unnecessary treatment or inflated billing. Competition generally benefits consumers through lower prices and redistributes gains away from sellers, while concentrating customers among fewer sellers in a period. Reputation without institutional safeguards increases consumer trust and seller business, but does not increase consumer profits in the reported comparison. The experiment uses students in abstract seller and consumer roles rather than actual professionals or clients. It offers no direct findings on lawyers, law firms, legal departments, ALSPs or AI vendors.
